overview: Tla-o-qui-aht homeland lies around Meares Island, Tofino and Long Beach on Vancouver Island’s west coast, extending inland beyond Sutton Pass. Fishing, carving, singing and dancing connect community life with this territory. Tla-o-qui-aht people continue to govern, teach and care for their lands and waters.

periods.title: Protecting Meares Island
periods.summary: Moses Martin declared the first Tribal Park in 1984 against proposed clear-cut logging. Community action combined peaceful blockades, legal proceedings and Indigenous governance.

periods.title: Guardians and restoration
periods.summary: The contemporary Tribal Parks Guardians programme began in 2008, continuing older responsibilities for land and water through monitoring, restoration and visitor guidance.

periods.title: A pathway with British Columbia
periods.summary: A process agreement signed on October 14, 2021 established a framework for discussions with British Columbia. The Nation presents this work as an assertion of its inherent authority.

periods.title: A further agreement with Canada
periods.summary: On June 27, 2024, Tla-o-qui-aht signed a memorandum of understanding with Canada. This provided another framework for negotiations about community priorities and government relationships.

items.text: The Nation describes traditional place names as records of occupation and cultural use. Some protected places have particular conditions of access, guided by the Ha’wiih. Knowing the landscape includes understanding responsibilities toward places, beyond knowing how to reach them.

Ha’wiih, the hereditary chiefs, hold responsibilities for lands, resources and cultural activities. The Nation describes this leadership as a continuing part of its governance. Territorial care and cultural life are linked in these responsibilities.

Guardians restore river and salmon habitat, monitor activities, maintain trails and remove invasive plants and marine debris. The programme brings ecological knowledge into paid work and practical care of places also visited by tourists.

The Tribal Parks report describes salmon hatchery work involving Chinook and coho, as well as habitat restoration. Such projects link fisheries with care for waterways. The account documents activities; it does not establish a measured recovery of every fish population.

Other reported projects include maintaining the Big Tree Trail boardwalk, involving Junior Guardians and providing food hampers during the COVID period. Visitor infrastructure, youth learning and household support all form part of the programme’s community work.

sections.title: Canoes, carving and the transmission of skill

items.text: Tutakwisnapšiƛ, Joe Martin, is a Tla-o-qui-aht Elder and master dugout-canoe carver. The Royal BC Museum describes his contribution to renewing canoe making in his own Nation and neighbouring communities. A working craft survives through skilled people who practise and share it.

Reflecting on museum collections, Martin described belongings removed during the suppression of potlatches and argued that some had been confiscated rather than freely collected. His account places the objects within histories of families, ceremony and colonial power.

Artist Joe David was born at Opitsaht and later studied and worked in art beyond his home community. His training included relationships with Bill Holm and Duane Pasco. The Museum of Anthropology held a solo exhibition of his work in 1978.

A small wooden mask by Joe David in the Metropolitan Museum is dated to 1981 to 1988. Painted surfaces and carved form are both part of the work. Its recorded maker and date show an individual artist working within a living artistic tradition.

Douglas David’s Chihaa mask, representing an eagle as a young boy, combines wood and paint with cedar bark, animal hair, abalone shell and leather. The Burke Museum’s catalogue records carving, painting and joining as parts of making this particular object.

sections.title: Keeping language and community knowledge accessible

items.text: A 2023 language-technology job posting described transferring cassette tapes, VHS recordings and documents into digital formats. The work included organizing audio and video and recording information about each item. Careful archival work helps keep recordings of fluent Elders usable for later learning.

The reconciliation process established in 2022 included elected and hereditary representatives, advisers and Elders. Its published approach brings proposals back to the community for discussion. Negotiation is connected to local priorities for services, well-being and future generations.

ending.text: Tla-o-qui-aht continues as a living Nation. Its agreements with British Columbia and Canada establish processes for negotiating relationships and community needs. They should not be read as the end of its people, a surrender of its asserted inherent authority or a completed final settlement.
